content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, darkness primarily symbolizes evil, sin, and spiritual separation from God — the moral and spiritual condition opposed to God, who is symbolized by light. It encompasses spiritual ignorance or blindness, the realm and power of Satan, and life apart from the truth and salvation revealed in Christ. Believers are described as being delivered 'out of darkness' into God's light, and unbelief or wickedness is portrayed as 'walking in darkness.'","primary_basis":["John 1:5","John 3:19-20","John 8:12","1 John 1:5-6","1 John 2:9-11","Ephesians 5:8-11","Ephesians 6:12","Colossians 1:13","Acts 26:18","1 Peter 2:9","Romans 13:12","1 Thessalonians 5:4-5","2 Corinthians 4:6","2 Corinthians 6:14","Isaiah 9:2","Matthew 4:16"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Divine judgment and eschatological punishment — darkness as an expression or setting of God's wrath, including the plague of darkness in Egypt, the darkness of the Day of the Lord, and the 'outer darkness' of final condemnation.","basis":["Exodus 10:21-23","Amos 5:18-20","Joel 2:1-2","Zephaniah 1:15","Matthew 8:12","Matthew 22:13","Matthew 25:30","Matthew 27:45","2 Peter 2:17","Jude 13","Revelation 16:10"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Death, the grave, and Sheol — darkness as the condition of the dead and the shadowed realm beyond life ('the shadow of death').","basis":["Job 10:21-22","Psalm 23:4","Psalm 88:6, 12","Psalm 107:10","Ecclesiastes 6:4","Luke 1:79"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Primordial chaos or the unformed state before God's creative ordering — darkness over the face of the deep prior to the creation of light.","basis":["Genesis 1:2-4","Isaiah 45:7","Jeremiah 4:23"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The hiddenness, mystery, and transcendence of God — God is said to dwell in 'thick darkness,' a strand developed in apophatic and mystical theology (e.g., Gregory of Nyssa, Pseudo-Dionysius, John of the Cross's 'dark night of the soul') where darkness signifies the incomprehensibility of God rather than evil.","basis":["Exodus 20:21","Deuteronomy 4:11","1 Kings 8:12","2 Chronicles 6:1","Psalm 18:11","Psalm 97:2"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Human suffering, affliction, or trial — darkness as a season of distress, despair, or testing through which the believer passes, distinct from moral evil.","basis":["Isaiah 50:10","Psalm 88 (throughout)","Job 19:8","Micah 7:8","Lamentations 3:2"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Secrecy or concealment in a neutral sense — things done or spoken 'in the dark' as hidden matters that will be exposed, without darkness itself being evil.","basis":["Luke 12:2-3","1 Corinthians 4:5","Matthew 10:27"],"prominence":"rare"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"Darkness is one of the most stable and widely recognized symbols in Christian interpretation, functioning almost universally as the antithesis of light in a dualistic light/darkness motif especially prominent in Johannine and Pauline literature. The primary meaning (evil, sin, ignorance, separation from God) is treated as dominant across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions and in standard reference works (e.g., Dictionary of Biblical Imagery). The alternative senses are not competing definitions so much as distinct biblical usages acknowledged alongside the dominant one; the apophatic/mystical reading (darkness as divine mystery) is the most notable interpretive counterpoint because it assigns darkness a positive rather than negative valence, but it remains a minority strand associated chiefly with contemplative and Eastern Christian traditions."}
